Hillbillies and rednecks are both country folk who live far from the cities and spend a lot of time maintaining a relatively simple lifestyle, taking care of their own property and needs rather than relying on paid goods and services.

If that's how they're similar, the way that they're different is the result of the environments they live in, but it shows up in their behavior.

"Redneck" comes from the stereotype of a sunburned neck from hours spent out under the sun. These folk hail from the plains or gentle hills, surrounded by miles and miles of fields and pastures. Once upon a time, these would have been the farmers that toil in the fields, but after the US government put a lot of money into state-funded education, farming became more and more efficient over time and less and less of the plains-dwellers had to make their living from manual labor on the farms. Outdoors living is a lifestyle that is hard to get away from, though, so instead of moving away from the rural plains and hills, these folks tended to stay in place and just change occupations - either using their technical and social skills to serve those who still owned and worked the land, or commuting long distance to work a job in a city and return home to the middle of nowhere for rest and leisure.

As an example, my maternal grandfather was an appliance salesman and general handyman - he didn't spend much time in the city, but rather traveled countless miles to to keep farmers and their wives happily supplied with operational machinery. His wife - before she became a homemaker and matriarch of the family - lived in the country, but traveled to the Iowa State University campus for her work. Their son today works for a major farming and earth-moving machine manufacturer, and one of their daughters sells equestrian equipment - saddles, bridles, medicine, etc.

These are not people who "live off the land" the way their ancestors did, but they still live in the family homes, doing the technical and service jobs that city-dwellers don't do. In their downtime, they go and do the things their families have always done: They fish, they shoot, they work on cars, what-have-you.

Hillbillies, by contrast, live in regions of much rougher hills or mountains, typically in deep woods. These are not places where the land produces a lot of value through farming, so you don't see the same effect where the farmers got much richer and started demanding goods and services. Instead, these people live directly off the land. If they're lucky, that means they have oil wells, gas wells, or valuable forest that provide a good income. If not, they scratch out a subsistence lifestyle by hunting and gathering valuable animal and plant products from the forest. A large portion of this goes directly to feeding the family, and the products that they can sell provide just enough money to buy the necessities that can't be taken from the forest.

Hillbilly communities are some of the most poverty-stricken areas in the US, but unlike the urban poor, hillbillies can actually make reasonable lives for themselves by their own efforts exploiting the resources around them. Their communities tend to be tight-knit and insular. At their best, hillbillies have very sharp senses, able bodies, and the kind of cunning it takes to survive at the ragged edges of civilization. At their worst, they're uneducated, idiosyncratic in the extreme, and too poor to scrape together emergency or retirement funds for when their bodies fail them.

To give you some interesting geographical context, there are plenty of self-declared 'necks in California who live in the suburbs. You're not a hillbilly unless you're at least 20 miles outside any city limits. Generally, a hillbilly can drink a 'neck under the table, and is more likely to be down with 420 out here. There's also some likelyhood of meth, but generally that moves them into the tweaker category because it renders them pretty non-functional and they often end up forced into the suburbs and onto the social welfare rolls, and then start calling themselves rednecks... but neither group really associates with them at that point.

Hillbillies generally know how to ride, drive a tractor, run a farm and regularly call the 'necks on their bullshit. Both own guns, but the 'necks are more likely show them off. A 'neck shoots at a shooting range, a hillbilly shoots wild turkey on his farm. A 'neck goes mudding on the weekend, a hillbilly goes mudding to work... when he's not driving his tractor, that is. Rednecks out here are likely to go for the blue collar work - welder, plumber, cops, sanitation engineer, etc. Most of them don't know how to run a farm or really live outside a suburban context - they're more glorifying country music and the image of the lifestyle. Hillbillies tend to be ok with hippies as long as they leave well enough alone and shut the fuck up. Rednecks will beat up hippies if they feel like it, and mock them. Rednecks tend to get in trouble with the law a lot more as well, probably because there's a lot more law around where they live.

Both groups tend to be bluntly honest, Christan, and generally overall good people. I've hung out with both (although I'm neither), and generally find myself liking the hillbillies more because they tend to be less about showing off how country they are... probably because they don't have to.

Note that this is a Northern Californian context, which is not the place you'd consider either group as really existing or originating, but both groups have been here longer than anyone save the Native Americans and the original Mexican settler families.
